planting.note: Set rhizome divisions shallowly in late summer to early fall so plants root in before the spring bloom cycle begins.

directions: Registered by P. O'Connor in 1999, Andouille carries one of the playful Cajun-culture names long traditional among Louisiana iris hybridizers, a group known for naming new introductions after regional food, places, and folklore. Grow it like other Louisiana iris: in rich, constantly moist to wet, slightly acidic soil along a pond margin, ditch bank, or low rain garden spot. Give it full sun to light shade and keep the planting from drying out through the growing season, dividing crowded clumps every few years in late summer.

planting.note: Divide and reset rhizomes in fall to let roots establish before the following spring's bloom stalks emerge.

directions: Hybridized by Heather Pryor and registered in 2004, Southern Star is one of many introductions from a breeder whose named cultivars are already well represented among Louisiana iris collections. Plant divisions in heavy, moisture-retentive soil enriched with organic matter, in a spot that stays damp to occasionally flooded. Full sun produces the heaviest bloom, though the planting tolerates light afternoon shade in hotter climates. Lift and separate the rhizome fans every three to four years once the clump becomes congested.

planting.note: Set out divisions in early fall into consistently wet ground so they are well rooted before winter dormancy.

directions: Bred by Peter Jackson from a cross of 'Tarawera Flow' and 'Little Ruby Slippers' and registered in 2018, Electric Storm is a more recent addition to the modern wave of Louisiana iris breeding that emphasizes bold, eye-catching patterning. Like other Louisiana iris, it performs best in heavy, fertile soil kept evenly saturated, whether at a pond edge, in a bog garden, or in a low spot that collects runoff. Provide full sun for strongest bloom and divide the expanding rhizome clump every few years to maintain vigor and flowering.

planting.note: Reset divided rhizomes shallow in fall, firming them into moist soil so new roots can anchor before spring growth.

directions: Overdressed was hybridized by P. O'Connor and registered in 2017, part of a steady stream of new Louisiana iris introductions bred for exhibition-quality flowers. Site it where the soil stays consistently moist to wet and is rich in organic matter, such as a rain garden, pond margin, or seasonally damp low spot. It flowers most heavily in full sun but tolerates part shade in warmer regions. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in late summer to keep the planting blooming well.

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall into saturated, humus-rich soil so the fans are rooted in before the next bloom season.

directions: Registered by hybridizer S. Poole in 2019, Jerry's Boutonniere is one of the newer Louisiana iris introductions recognized by the Society for Louisiana Irises. Grow it as you would other Louisiana iris: in heavy, constantly moist to wet, slightly acidic soil, ideally at a pond edge, bog garden, or low-lying bed that collects water. Full sun yields the strongest bloom, and the clump should be lifted and divided every few years once growth becomes crowded.

planting.note: Install rhizome divisions in early fall in wet, fertile ground to allow full root establishment before winter.

directions: Hybridized by Heather Pryor and registered in 2001, Wow Factor is another of this prolific breeder's named Louisiana iris introductions. It thrives in rich, consistently moist to wet soil along pond edges, drainage ditches, or any low garden spot that stays damp. Full sun brings on the heaviest flowering, though the plant tolerates part-day shade in hot climates. Divide the rhizome clump every three to four years to keep flowering vigorous.

planting.note: Set divisions shallowly into saturated soil in fall so they establish ahead of the spring bloom flush.

directions: Registered by P. O'Connor in 2013, Cocodrie takes its name from a Cajun word for wild bayou country, continuing the Louisiana iris tradition of names drawn from regional geography and dialect. Grow it in heavy, moisture-retentive soil kept consistently wet, such as a bog garden or pond margin, and give it full sun for the best flowering display. Lift and divide the expanding clump every few years once it becomes crowded to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall in constantly damp soil to let roots take hold before the following spring.

directions: Registered by Sally Smith in 1947, Royal Gem is one of the earliest Louisiana iris cultivars recognized after the Society for Louisiana Irises began systematically documenting hybrids in the 1940s. As an older selection from that founding generation, it helped establish the breeding lines behind many later award winners. Grow it in heavy, fertile soil kept consistently moist to wet, giving it full sun and dividing the clump every three to four years as it fills in.

planting.note: Set rhizome divisions shallow in fall into wet, humus-rich soil so they root before next spring's bloom.

directions: Registered by Lillian Trichel in 1950 and named for the Caddo Lake region of northwest Louisiana, this cultivar belongs to the founding generation of named Louisiana iris that the Society for Louisiana Irises helped bring into cultivation, winning a Society Honorable Mention plus the DeBaillon Award that same year. Give it rich, consistently moist to wet soil, full sun, and the same bog-garden or pond-edge conditions that suit other Louisiana iris. Divide the rhizome clump every few years once it becomes crowded to sustain strong bloom.

planting.note: Plant divisions in early fall in saturated soil so the clump is established before the next bloom cycle.

directions: Named and distributed by Victorine Kraemer in 1943, Kraemer Yellow was among the first yellow-flowered selections of the giganticaerulea form recognized by early Louisiana iris growers, and it went on to serve as a productive parent in later breeding programs. Treat it like any Louisiana iris, planting divisions in rich, wet to constantly moist soil in full sun. Divide the expanding rhizome fans every few years to maintain strong flowering.

planting.note: Set out divisions in fall into consistently wet soil to root in well before the following spring.

directions: Registered by George Arceneaux in 1945, Louise Austin is a named Iris fulva x Iris foliosa hybrid clone counted among the foundational Louisiana iris cultivars that hybridizers repeatedly used as breeding stock during the formative decades of organized Louisiana iris development. Give it the same culture as other Louisiana iris: heavy, fertile, consistently moist to wet soil, full sun, and periodic division of the rhizome clump every three to four years to keep it blooming well.

planting.note: Plant divisions shallowly in fall into wet, fertile soil so roots establish before spring bloom.

directions: Registered by Benny Trahan Sr. in 2012, King Alex is grown in heavy, consistently moist to wet soil in full sun, the same conditions favored by all Louisiana iris. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years in late summer to keep the display strong.

planting.note: Install rhizome divisions in fall in saturated, fertile soil to establish before the next bloom season.

directions: Bred by Joseph Musacchia from a cross of 'Mac's Blue Heaven' and 'In the Navy' and registered in 2019, Mama Janice went on to win the Society for Louisiana Irises' Marie Caillet Cup. Culture is the same as for other Louisiana iris: rich, consistently wet to moist soil, full sun, and division of the rhizome clump every few years to sustain vigorous bloom.

planting.note: Set out divisions in fall into consistently wet soil so they are well rooted ahead of spring growth.

directions: Another Joe Musacchia introduction, Cajun Jester is grown like other Louisiana iris in heavy, fertile, consistently moist to wet soil under full sun, dividing the rhizome clump every three to four years as it fills in.

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall in wet, humus-rich soil to establish roots ahead of the following spring.

directions: Hybridized by Peter Jackson, Mississippi Eavesdropper is noted for its pendant flower form, with falls and standards that droop downward rather than flaring flat or standing upright, a shape found partway along the range of Louisiana iris flower structures. Grow it in rich, consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in full sun, the standard conditions for Louisiana iris, and divide the clump every three to four years to keep it blooming vigorously.
